summary: The submission sets out its literature honestly. It says each dissection is classical, follows from the Dehn-Sydler theorem or from Debrunner (1980), or already appears in the recreational dissection literature, and it claims only that these explicit dissections are machine-checked. That leaves a finite list of exact instances of a known existence theorem. No new mathematical statement, no general theorem, and no method that carries beyond the listed solids. The submission does not show that this family of instances could plausibly warrant a research paper, and it names no research audience for the instances beyond the formalization itself. The research-interest requirement is therefore not affirmatively established. Separately, one sub-family of the listed solids is named with no source.

findings.evidence: inputs/E1-explicit-scissors-congruences.md: 'What is claimed' and 'Limits stated by the submitter'
findings.message: The result group is a finite collection of explicit scissors congruences between named solids and cubes. The submission itself says these are classical, follow from Sydler (1965) or Debrunner (1980), or are already in the recreational literature (Frederickson's ch. 20 updates; Wolfram Demonstrations). The only contribution claimed is that the explicit pieces are machine-checked. Policy section 1 says formal correctness and the size of a Lean development do not by themselves establish research interest. The submission does not show that these instances support a research paper or serious note, and it names no specialist audience that would find these particular dissections interesting as mathematics. Neither research-interest test is affirmatively established. Better prose would not fix this. What would: a general statement in place of instances, for example a constructive Sydler direction for a stated class such as all parallelohedra or all polyhedra whose dihedral angles are rational multiples of π, with an audience identified for it.

The family 'the nine "most regular" space-fillers' and the solid called 'the Bain rhombic dodecahedron' are introduced without a source. The count of nine, the classification into four parallelepipeds, two hexagonal prisms, a rhombic dodecahedron, an elongated dodecahedron and the truncated octahedron, and the name 'Bain' are given with no citation and no proof that the list is complete. An independent search found no standard source for this family or this name. Because the family defines what the result group covers, either cite where the classification comes from or present it as the submission's own enumeration, with its derivation and the standard names of the solids.

internal_notes.message: The classical account is accurate: Dehn 1901, Sydler 1965, Jessen 1968's tensor form, Debrunner 1980 (tilers have zero Dehn invariant and are scissors congruent to a cube), and Lagarias-Moews 1995 (doi checked by citation). Citations are exact. Sources not read (Sah 1979, Debrunner read only through citations) are disclosed precisely, which policy permits.

Spot check passes: cube-cube faces meet at 90°, rhombic dodecahedron faces at 120°, and cube face against rhombic dodecahedron face (normals at 45°) at 135°. All are rational multiples of π, so the Dehn invariant is zero for every member of the family.
Confirmed: Theobald 12 pieces (improving Hanegraaf) and 11 pieces (Oct 2007) for truncated octahedron to cube. The submission's attribution is correct.

Independent searches found no formalization of Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien, of Sydler's theorem, or of a Dehn invariant in Lean, Isabelle, Coq or elsewhere, apart from what the submission names. Searching cannot prove absence. The Lean Zulip and FormalBook were not inspected directly.

Could also cite: Dupont and Sah on the homological view of scissors congruence; Hadwiger's work on box-to-cube and parallelohedron equidecomposability (the box-to-cube step is classical and could be credited to him); Boltianskii, Hilbert's Third Problem (1978), for constructive equidecomposition of prisms and parallelepipeds. None of these changes the public account.

The best case for an audience is formal-geometry researchers who want kernel-checked constructive certificates. Even so, instances do not reach the paper-worthiness bar unless the construction is uniform or general. A machine-checked Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien in the plane, or a uniform constructive proof for all parallelohedra, would be a materially stronger candidate.

what_would_reach_higher: Replace the list of instances with a general theorem proved uniformly, for example: every parallelohedron, or every polyhedron that tiles space by translates, is scissors congruent to a cube of the same volume, with the pieces constructed by a stated algorithm. That turns instances of Debrunner's existence result into a constructive formal theorem with a clear audience in scissors congruence and formal geometry.

As a stepping stone, formalize the Wallace-Bolyai-Gerwien theorem in the plane in general, together with its 3D corollary for prisms and boxes (box to cube). No formalization of either was found, and both are standard theorems rather than single instances.

State an identified research audience and a paper-worthy question that the explicit certificates answer, for example certified minimal or bounded piece counts, or a general bound on piece count in terms of the combinatorics of the solid. Without one, the instances read as recreational.

Cite or derive the 'nine most regular space-fillers' classification, prove the enumeration complete, and give each solid its standard name with discoverer. Replace or source the name 'Bain rhombic dodecahedron'.
Credit the classical constructive steps at the point of use: Hadwiger and Boltianskii for prism and box equidecomposability, and Dupont-Sah for the algebraic framework.
Build the proof and record the Comparator configuration so the planned statements can be checked against actual declarations.
